title: Psalm 146: Put Not Your Trust in Princes
summary: The psalmist vows to praise the LORD as long as he lives and warns against trusting princes, mortal men whose plans die with them. Blessed is the one whose help and hope is the God of Jacob, Maker of heaven and earth, who remains faithful forever. The LORD executes justice for the oppressed, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, opens blind eyes, lifts the bowed down, protects foreigners, sustains the fatherless and widow, and frustrates the wicked. The LORD reigns forever.
story: Psalm 146 is the first of the five Hallelujah psalms (Psalms 146 to 150) that close the Psalter, each beginning and ending with Hallelujah. It comes immediately after Psalm 145, the last psalm of David, which ended with the call for every creature to bless God's holy name. Psalm 146 answers with one voice, the psalmist's own soul, and the praise will widen through the next four psalms until everything that has breath praises the LORD (Psalm 150:6). Its warning against trusting princes is striking after the royal psalms of the final Davidic collection: the Psalter's last word on kingship is that only the LORD reigns forever.
historical:
The psalm has no Hebrew superscription beyond the opening Hallelujah. Some manuscripts of the Septuagint attribute Psalms 146 to 148 to the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who ministered in Jerusalem around 520 BC after the return from exile, but that attribution is not in the Hebrew text and most scholars treat it as a later tradition. Many scholars date the psalm to the Persian period after the exile, when Judah had no king of its own and lived under foreign rulers. In that setting the warning against trusting princes would have had special force. Others see it as fitting any period when human leaders failed God's people.

The psalm's description of God's care for the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, foreigners, the fatherless, and the widow draws on the law and the prophets (Deuteronomy 10:18 and Isaiah 61:1). These were the people the king was meant to defend, and the psalm says the LORD does what human kings so often failed to do.
cultural:
Princes in the ancient world held power over life and death, and people naturally looked to them for protection, favor, and justice. The psalm's warning reflects a world where alliances with powerful men could seem the surest security. But the princes too were mortal. When his spirit departs (verse 4), a ruler returns to the ground, echoing God's words to Adam that he would return to the dust (Genesis 3:19), and on that day all his plans come to nothing.

The list in verses 7 to 9 names the most vulnerable people in ancient society. The fatherless and the widow had no male protector in a world where legal standing, property, and safety depended on one. Foreigners (sojourners, resident aliens) lived without the protection of kin or land rights. Prisoners, often debtors or captives of war, were at the mercy of their captors. The blind could rarely work and often begged. Israel's law commanded special care for such people (Exodus 22:21-24 and Deuteronomy 24:17-22), because the LORD himself cared for them.
literary: Psalm 146 is a hymn of praise framed by Hallelujah at beginning and end. Verses 1 and 2 are the psalmist's personal vow to praise. Verses 3 and 4 are a warning, set in contrast with verse 5's beatitude: blessed is the one whose help is the God of Jacob. Verses 6 to 9 describe God's character and works in a series of short participle clauses, each describing what the LORD does, with the divine name repeated at the start of several lines for emphasis (verses 7 to 9). Verse 10 closes with the declaration that the LORD reigns forever. The psalm's movement from human mortality to divine permanence mirrors its contrast between trusting princes and trusting God.

outline.t: I will praise the LORD all my life
Do not trust in mortal princes
Blessed is the one whose help is the God of Jacob
What the LORD does for the vulnerable

doctrines.note: The psalm contrasts trust in mortal rulers with trust in the everlasting God. Faith is not merely belief but reliance, placing one's hope and help in the one who remains faithful forever.
The LORD reigns forever, and his reign is marked by justice for the oppressed and care for the vulnerable. The psalm describes God's kingdom by what he does for those human kingdoms overlook.
Trusting princes is a subtle form of idolatry: looking to a creature for what only God can give. The psalm warns against placing ultimate hope in any human leader, however powerful.

words.note: Nadiv, noble or prince. The word describes people of rank and influence, those with power to help or harm. Verse 3 warns against trusting them because they are mortal. The same warning appears in Psalm 118:9, which says it is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.

Ruach, spirit or breath. In verse 4 it describes the breath of life that leaves a person at death. When the breath departs, a prince returns to the ground. The word recalls God breathing life into the first human (Genesis 2:7), and the psalm reminds readers that even the most powerful ruler depends on breath God gives.

Ezer, help or helper. The word describes someone who comes to the aid of another, and it is often used of God as Israel's helper (Psalm 121:1-2). In Genesis 2:18 the same word describes the woman as a helper for the man, not implying inferiority, since God himself is called a helper. Here the one whose help is the God of Jacob is blessed.

Ger, sojourner or foreigner. The word describes a resident alien, someone living in a land not his own, without inherited rights. Israel was commanded to care for the ger because Israel had been foreigners in Egypt (Exodus 22:21). The LORD protects them.

christ: When Jesus began his ministry in Nazareth, he read from Isaiah 61, announcing good news to the poor, freedom for prisoners, recovery of sight for the blind, and release for the oppressed (Luke 4:18-19). When John the Baptist's disciples asked whether Jesus was the one to come, he pointed to the blind receiving sight, the lame walking, and the poor hearing good news (Matthew 11:4-5). These are the very works Psalm 146 attributes to the LORD. The psalm says that the LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the Gospels show Jesus doing it. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 146 directly, but it presents Jesus as doing what the psalm says only God does, which is part of how the early church came to confess him as Lord. The psalm's warning against trusting mortal princes finds its answer in the one Prince who died and did not remain in the ground.
questions: The psalm warns against trusting princes. Where are you tempted to place your hope in a leader, a party, or a powerful person?
The LORD's care is described by what he does for the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, foreigners, orphans, and widows. What does that list tell you about what God values?
The psalmist vows to praise God as long as he lives. What would it look like to make praise a lifelong habit rather than an occasional response?
